q-87745.name: Question 1
q-87745.worked_solution:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)-5} & \ge {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)}\cdot {e}^{-5} & \ge {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)} \\ (x+2){e}^{-5} & \ge 3x \\ x+2 & \ge 3{e}^{5}x \\ 2 & \ge (3{e}^{5}-1)x \\ \frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1} & \ge x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >-2 \\ 3x & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >0\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x\le \frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1},$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,\frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1}].$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>-2$ and $x>0,$ which can be expressed as $(-2,\infty )$ and $(0,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,\frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1}]\cap (-2,\infty )\cap (0,\infty )=(0,\frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1}]
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (0,\frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1}],$ which can also be written as $0<x\le \frac{2}{3{e}^{5}-1}.$

q-87745.html:
Question 1
?

Solve the inequality ln⁡(x+2)−5≥ln⁡(3x).

a
x≤23e5−1
b
−23e5−1≤x≤0
c
 −23e5−1≤x≤23e5−1
d
 x≥23e5−1
e
 0<x≤23e5−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of e. This gives the following:

eln⁡(x+2)−5≥eln⁡(3x)eln⁡(x+2)⋅e−5≥eln⁡(3x)(x+2)e−5≥3xx+2≥3e5x2≥(3e5−1)x23e5−1≥x

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

x+2>0⇒x>−23x>0⇒x>0

Our solution is x≤23e5−1, which can be expressed as (−∞,23e5−1]. Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are x>−2 and x>0, which can be expressed as (−2,∞) and (0,∞) respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

(−∞,23e5−1]∩(−2,∞)∩(0,∞)=(0,23e5−1]

Therefore, the solution is x∈(0,23e5−1], which can also be written as 0<x≤23e5−1.

q-88006.name: Question 2
q-88006.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the logarithm:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)+4 & \ge 0 \\ \frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2) & \ge -4 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2) & \ge -6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)} & \ge {e}^{-6} \\ x-2 & \ge {e}^{-6} \\ x & \ge {e}^{-6}+2 \\ x & \ge \frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x-2>0\,⇒\,x>2
$$

Our solution is $x\ge \frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}},$ which can be expressed as $[\frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}},\infty ).$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x>2,$ which can be expressed as $(2,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
[\frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}},\infty )\cap (2,\infty )=[\frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}},\infty )
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in [\frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}},\infty ),$ which can also be written as $x\ge \frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}}.$

eln⁡(x−2)≥e−6x−2≥e−6x≥e−6+2x≥1+2e6e6

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

x−2>0⇒x>2

Our solution is x≥1+2e6e6, which can be expressed as [1+2e6e6,∞). Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is x>2, which can be expressed as (2,∞). To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

[1+2e6e6,∞)∩(2,∞)=[1+2e6e6,∞)

q-102969.name: Question 3
q-102969.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the logarithm:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}⁡(4x-6)-1 & \le 0 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡(4x-6) & \le 1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $10.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(4x-6)} & \le {10}^{1} \\ 4x-6 & \le 10 \\ 4x & \le 16 \\ x & \le 4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
4x-6>0\,⇒\,x>\frac{3}{2}
$$

Our solution is $x\le 4,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,4].$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x>\frac{3}{2},$ which can be expressed as $(\frac{3}{2},\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,4]\cap (\frac{3}{2},\infty )=(\frac{3}{2},4]
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (\frac{3}{2},4],$ which can also be written as $\frac{3}{2}<x\le 4.$

Our solution is x≤4, which can be expressed as (−∞,4]. Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is x>32, which can be expressed as (32,∞). To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection: (−∞,4]∩(32,∞)=(32,4]

Therefore, the solution is x∈(32,4], which can also be written as 32<x≤4.

q-276950.name: Question 4
q-276950.worked_solution:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $10.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(2-x)+1} & \le {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(x+9)} \\ {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(2-x)}\cdot {10}^{1} & \le {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(x+9)} \\ (2-x)\cdot 10 & \le x+9 \\ 20-10x & \le x+9 \\ -11x & \le -11 \\ x & \ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}2-x & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & <2 \\ x+9 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >-9\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x\ge 1,$ which can be expressed as $[1,\infty ).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x<2$ and $x>-11,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,2)$ and $(-11,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
[1,\infty )\cap (-\infty ,2)\cap (-9,\infty )=[1,2)
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in [1,2),$ which can also be written as $1\le x<2.$

q-278762.name: Question 5
q-278762.worked_solution:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)} & \ge {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-2x)-3} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)} & \ge {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-2x)}\cdot {e}^{-3} \\ (x+1) & \ge (4-2x)\cdot \frac{1}{{e}^{3}} \\ {e}^{3}(x+1) & \ge 4-2x \\ x{e}^{3}+{e}^{3} & \ge 4-2x \\ {e}^{3}-4 & \ge -2x-x{e}^{3} \\ {e}^{3}-4 & \ge -x(2+{e}^{3}) \\ \frac{{e}^{3}-4}{2+{e}^{3}} & \ge -x \\ x & \ge \frac{4-{e}^{3}}{2+{e}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >-1 \\ 4-2x & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & <2\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x\ge \frac{4-{e}^{3}}{2+{e}^{3}},$ which can be expressed as $[\frac{4-{e}^{3}}{2+{e}^{3}},\infty ).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>-1$ and $x<2,$ which can be expressed as $(-1,\infty )$ and $(-\infty ,2)$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
[\frac{4-{e}^{3}}{2+{e}^{3}},\infty )\cap (-1,\infty )\cap (-\infty ,2)=[\frac{4-{e}^{3}}{2+{e}^{3}},2)
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in [\frac{4-{e}^{3}}{2+{e}^{3}},2),$ which can also be written as 

$$
\frac{4-{e}^{3}}{2+{e}^{3}}\le x<2.
$$
